title: Eligibility traces and temporal credit assignment

html:
The most consequential feature of the SPN dendritic spine, from the standpoint of reinforcement learning, is that it provides an architecture for eligibility traces–the molecular memory of recent synaptic coactivation on which a temporally delayed teaching signal can act. The distal reward problem ("how does a dopaminergic burst arriving hundreds of milliseconds to seconds after the action know which synapses participated?") is solved, at the corticostriatal spine, by a cascade of biochemical events that outlast the initial pre-post coincidence and decay on a timescale matched to the physiological delay of the reward signal.

The distal reward problem is among the oldest puzzles in learning theory. In neural terms, the difficulty is acute: the firing patterns that represent a sensory cue or motor act occur on a millisecond timescale; these patterns are typically no longer present in the network when the dopaminergic teaching signal arrives seconds later; and that teaching signal is broadcast diffusely across many synapses, most of which did not participate in the relevant action 1. The theoretical resolution, proposed long before it was experimentally demonstrated, is that nearly coincident pre- and postsynaptic activity leaves behind a slowly decaying synaptic tag–an eligibility trace–that marks recently active synapses as candidates for modification without itself changing synaptic efficacy. Only when a neuromodulatory reinforcement signal arrives during the lifetime of the trace is the tag converted into lasting potentiation or depression. The trace is "silent" in the sense that, absent the third factor, no net synaptic change occurs; the synapse is merely rendered eligible for change 1, 2. This three-factor architecture–Hebbian coincidence (factor one), postsynaptic depolarization or calcium (factor two), and delayed neuromodulator (factor three)–maps directly onto the temporal-difference learning rule: the eligibility trace plays the role of the decaying memory e(s,a)e(s,a) that allows the scalar error δ\delta to update the weight of the state-action pair that generated it, even when the error arrives after a delay 1, 2. A 2024 study tests sensory-reinforced corticostriatal plasticity (Figure) 22.

A decisive experimental demonstration of a corticostriatal eligibility trace came from Yagishita, Hayashi-Takagi, Ellis-Davies, and colleagues, who used two-photon glutamate uncaging at individual dendritic spines of D1R-expressing SPNs in nucleus accumbens slices, combined with optogenetic activation of dopaminergic fibres via channelrhodopsin-2, to independently control the timing of the glutamatergic and dopaminergic inputs to a single spine 3. An STDP protocol (repetitive glutamate uncaging paired with postsynaptic action potentials) alone produced only a modest and transient spine enlargement. When dopaminergic fibre stimulation was delivered within a narrow, asymmetric time window of approximately 0.3 to 2 seconds after the glutamatergic input, however, spine enlargement was dramatically and persistently enhanced—a structural correlate of long-term potentiation at the single-spine level 3. Importantly, dopamine delivered before the glutamatergic input, or more than about 2 seconds after it, had no potentiating effect, confirming that the trace is both temporally asymmetric and sharply bounded. This result constituted the first demonstration of reinforcement plasticity–the conjunction of Hebbian eligibility with delayed neuromodulatory gating–at the resolution of a single corticostriatal spine. A related experiment records corticostriatal synapses in vivo (Figure).

Shindou, Shindou, Watanabe, and Wickens provided a complementary and more direct test using whole-cell recordings from identified D1-expressing SPNs in dorsomedial striatum, with phasic dopamine release achieved by photolysis of caged dopamine at precisely controlled delays after pre-post spike-timing protocols 4. The key finding was that uncaging dopamine selectively at 2 seconds after pre-post pairing converted the outcome from long-term depression into net long-term potentiation, whereas dopamine delivered at earlier or later delays did not. The trace was electrophysiologically "silent"–no change in synaptic efficacy was detectable during the interval between the spike pairing and dopamine arrival–yet the synapse was nonetheless primed for potentiation, confirming the theoretical prediction of a silent eligibility trace 4. A molecular marker of this silent state was identified: pre-post pairings caused a transient increase in rectification (asymmetric flow of electrical current) consistent with insertion of calcium-permeable AMPA receptors (CP-AMPARs) into the postsynaptic membrane, lasting approximately 2-4 seconds after pairing, and a CP-AMPAR antagonist blocked dopamine-dependent t-LTP without affecting t-LTD 4. In parallel, Fisher, Reynolds, and colleagues demonstrated the eligibility trace in vivo in intact rats: pairing corticostriatal activity with a reward-conditioned sensory reinforcement signal (which drives dopamine release) induced robust bidirectional STDP at corticostriatal synapses, but only if the reinforcement signal arrived within approximately 2 seconds of the spike-timing pairing; the effect was dependent on both D1 and adenosine A2A receptor signaling 5. Taken together, the Yagishita, Shindou, and Fisher results converge on a consistent picture: the corticostriatal eligibility trace has a characteristic lifetime on the order of 1-2 seconds, it is synapse-specific in its initial induction but requires a temporally delayed neuromodulatory signal to be converted into lasting change, and it operates through distinct but complementary mechanisms depending on SPN subtype. A related in-vivo rat study tests reinforcement timing (Figure).

The molecular mechanism that shapes this narrow temporal window has now been constrained in considerable detail. The critical insight is that the temporal contingency between glutamatergic and dopaminergic inputs is detected by rapid regulation of cAMP in the thin distal dendrites where corticostriatal spines reside, with the effective time window emerging from a competition between calcium-sensitive adenylyl cyclase activity and high local phosphodiesterase activity 3, 6. Pre-post coincidence drives calcium influx into the spine, primarily through NMDA receptors and voltage-gated calcium channels, which primes calcium-sensitive adenylyl cyclase AC1 to produce cAMP. But the high phosphodiesterase activity that characterizes SPN dendrites rapidly degrades cAMP unless D1 receptor activation by dopamine arrives while AC1 is still calcium-primed–that is, within the  0.3-2 s window 3, 6. Only when the two signals converge within this interval does the cAMP transient overcome the PDE barrier, activating PKA and its downstream effectors, including DARPP-32-mediated inhibition of PP1, thereby permitting the stabilization of CaMKII-dependent spine enlargement and synaptic potentiation 3, 6. If dopamine arrives too late, spine calcium has decayed and the barrier cannot be overcome; if it arrives too early, the calcium signal has not yet occurred. The result is an AC1-centered, PDE-constrained molecular coincidence detector whose time constant defines the eligibility window 3, 6. Although calcium-sensitive adenylyl cyclases are expressed in dendritic spines across brain regions, and similar logic may operate wherever thin dendrites receive convergent activity-dependent and neuromodulatory signals, the striatum appears to be especially well tuned for this computation. Compared to cortical pyramidal neurons, striatal neurons exhibit much faster, larger, and longer-lasting cAMP/PKA responses to brief D1 stimulation–likely driven by faster cAMP production, lower PDE4-mediated degradation, and the presence of DARPP-32, which prolongs PKA action by inhibiting phosphatases 7. More broadly, SPNs are unusually dopamine-dependent plasticity substrates: unlike canonical cortical plasticity, which is often inducible through activity-dependent glutamatergic mechanisms alone and only variably gated by dopamine, many of the most behaviorally relevant forms of corticostriatal plasticity depend strongly on dopaminergic receptor activation, particularly in reinforcement-linked settings, even if this dependence is not absolute across every induction protocol or experimental preparation 8, 9. Whereas cortical neurons respond much more weakly and sluggishly to brief dopamine transients, striatal neurones are tuned to detect exactly the kind of sharp, phasic signal produced by reward prediction errors: a sub-second dopamine pulse that produces only modest responses in prefrontal pyramidal cells drives a robust PKA response in striatal medium spiny neurons 7. The implication is that the SPN is not merely a generic neuron that happens to receive dopamine; rather, its intracellular signaling architecture appears specialized for the detection of temporally precise reinforcement signals, making the striatal eligibility-trace mechanism exceptionally well matched to the temporal statistics of the dopaminergic teaching signal it is designed to capture 3, 6, 7, 8. The in-vivo study tests dopamine and adenosine signaling (Figure).

A behavioral correlate of the synaptic eligibility trace was demonstrated by Yamanaka, Bhatt, and colleagues, who showed that Pavlovian conditioning of head-fixed mice to pure tones depended on a reward-sensitive period of approximately 1 second after tone presentation, and that optogenetically induced presynaptic activity at nucleus accumbens synapses reproduced the same narrow sensitive window 10. The conditioning depended on plasticity-related signaling in the NAc, and the temporal profile of the behavioural sensitive period closely matched the synaptic eligibility trace measured in slice preparations, providing the first direct link between the subcellular molecular window and the timescale of reinforcement learning at the behavioural level 10.

The eligibility window at corticostriatal synapses, though brief, is broadly matched to the fast temporal profile of phasic dopaminergic teaching signals in reinforcement learning. In key striatal plasticity experiments, dopamine is effective within a narrow window on the order of  0.3–2 s after eligible glutamatergic activity 3, 4. Midbrain dopamine responses to unexpected rewards are themselves phasic and brief, and during learning these responses transfer from reward delivery to reward-predictive cues in a manner consistent with temporal-difference accounts 11, 12. Accordingly, for many single-step or short-delay tasks, this eligibility window is sufficient to bridge the gap between the corticostriatal activity involved in action selection and the dopaminergic signal that evaluates the outcome. The study varies the delay before sensory reinforcement (Figure). The 2024 study measures reinforced corticostriatal changes (Figure).

But many real-world learning problems involve delays that substantially exceed 2 seconds–multi-step action sequences, delayed feedback, and extended temporal gaps between choice and consequence. How does the BG solve temporal credit assignment on these longer timescales? The answer is almost certainly not a single mechanism but a layered set of solutions operating at different timescales, of which the synaptic eligibility trace is only the fastest. A computational model tests reinforced spike-timing-dependent plasticity (Figure). A review illustrates distinct temporal credit-assignment problems (Figure) 21.

The first and most important long-range mechanism is temporal-difference learning itself. The TD algorithm does not require that the ultimate reward signal reach back to the first action in a sequence; it requires only that each state’s prediction error update the value of the immediately preceding state. As cues and intermediate states acquire predictive value through experience, the dopaminergic teaching signal transfers backward in time—from reward delivery to the last predictive cue, from that cue to an earlier one, and so on. This backward propagation of value through the chain of states means that, in a well-learned task, the relevant dopaminergic error signal for any given action occurs not at the time of final reward but at the next state transition, which is typically within the 1–2 s eligibility window. TD chaining thus converts a long-horizon credit assignment problem into a series of short-horizon problems, each of which falls within the reach of the synaptic eligibility trace 1, 13. It is worth reiterating that the "states" over which this chaining operates are not limited to raw sensory surfaces. As established in the error-signal section, midbrain dopamine neurons compute prediction errors over cortically constructed belief states–latent task representations supplied by orbitofrontal cortex 14, hidden-state inferences shaped by medial prefrontal cortex 15, and even identity and associative-structure expectations updated through model-based inference 16, 17. This means that the intermediate states through which TD value propagates backward can be abstract, high-dimensional, and context-dependent—a cortical map of inferred task structure, not merely a chain of cached stimulus-response associations. The effective reach of backward chaining therefore reflects the richness of the state representation that cortex makes legible to the dopaminergic system. The in-vivo study also investigates action learning (Figure).

A second mechanism involves sustained neural activity in prefrontal and striatal circuits that effectively extends the representation of the relevant state across the delay period, keeping the "right" corticostriatal synapses active until the teaching signal arrives. Histed, Pasupathy, and Miller recorded single neurons in primate prefrontal cortex and caudate nucleus during learning of stimulus-response associations and found that both areas contained neurons with sustained, persistent outcome-related responses that lasted well beyond the immediate reward period and predicted the accuracy of subsequent choices 18. Her and colleagues further showed that dorsomedial and dorsolateral striatal neurons maintained choice-related signals across a delay period in a dynamic foraging task requiring temporal credit assignment, with choice signals appearing sequentially—first in DMS and then in DLS—and being combined with action value and reward signals in DLS at the time of outcome revelation 19. More recently, Wirt and colleagues demonstrated that medial prefrontal cortex neurons projecting to dorsomedial striatum show elevated activity during the maintenance period of working memory tasks, and that optogenetic inhibition of this projection during the delay selectively impaired performance, indicating that sustained prefrontal-to-striatal input functionally bridges the temporal gap between stimulus encoding and subsequent action 20. On this view, persistent corticostriatal activity does not replace the eligibility trace; it reactivates or sustains the synaptic input pattern across the delay, ensuring that when the dopaminergic signal finally arrives, the relevant corticostriatal synapses are still (or again) in an eligible state. The eligibility trace mechanism and sustained cortical drive are thus complementary: the trace handles delays up to 2̃ seconds at the synaptic level, while persistent prefrontal and striatal activity extends the effective reach of the same three-factor plasticity rule to longer timescales by maintaining the first factor (corticostriatal coactivation) until the third factor (dopamine) arrives 13. The in-vivo study examines striatal activity after a cue (Figure).

The picture that emerges is of a multi-timescale credit assignment architecture in which the synaptic eligibility trace, TD-mediated backward chaining of value, and sustained prefrontal-striatal activity jointly solve the temporal binding problem across a range of delays. At the shortest timescales (sub-second to  2 s), the molecular machinery of the SPN spine—calcium-sensitive adenylyl cyclase, phosphodiesterase gating, PKA-DARPP-32-PP1 signaling, and transient CP-AMPAR insertion—provides a synapse-autonomous eligibility window that is well matched to the latency of phasic dopamine bursts. At intermediate timescales (seconds to tens of seconds), TD propagation of value through state chains brings the relevant prediction error within reach of the eligibility window at each step. At still longer timescales, or in ambiguous multi-cue environments where eligibility traces alone would credit the wrong synapses, persistent prefrontal activity supplies a network-level "memory bridge" that keeps the relevant corticostriatal ensemble active across the delay. Together, these mechanisms ensure that the dopaminergic teaching signal–however delayed relative to the original action–can be directed to the synapses that actually participated in the behaviorally relevant computation, closing the loop from evaluative error to targeted, temporally precise policy update.
